This notebook is the map, not the analysis. The work was written one milestone at a time; the brief
asks for it organised by CRISP-DM phase, so each section below names the decision that phase settled
and points at the notebook, script or file that carries it. Nothing here re-runs or rewrites that
code: to reproduce a phase, knit the notebook it names. `notebook/BIN 381 Milestone 3 - Full
Notebook (Group P1).Rmd` runs modelling, evaluation and deployment end to end in one pass, and the
`README.md` has the clean-clone order for everything else.

Knitting this file checks that every artifact named below is actually in the repository.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)
root <- normalizePath(if (basename(getwd()) == "notebook") ".." else ".")

# One row per artifact. The table under each section is drawn from this, so a file that is
# renamed or lost shows up as MISSING when this notebook is knitted.
artifacts <- function(...) {
  a <- rbind(...)
  a <- data.frame(Phase = a[, 1], Artifact = a[, 2], Holds = a[, 3], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  a$Present <- ifelse(file.exists(file.path(root, a$Artifact)), "yes", "MISSING")
  a
}

MAP <- artifacts(
  c("Business understanding", "report/M4/BIN381_M4_Report_Group_P1.docx",
    "Section 1: the problem, the stakeholder, BO1-BO3 and H1-H6"),
  c("Business understanding", "report/M4/BIN381_M4_Handover_and_Maintenance.md",
    "Who owns what, known issues, retirement triggers"),

  c("Data preparation",

  c("Data preparation", "notebook/BIN 381 Milestone 2 Person A - Prepare for Modelling.Rmd",

  c("Data preparation", "data/clean/qa_log_personC.csv", "Every cleaning treatment, by column"),
  c("Data preparation", "data/integrated/M2_final_modelling_dataset.rds",
    "20,925 modelled households"),

phase <- function(p) knitr::kable(MAP[MAP$Phase == p, c("Artifact", "Holds", "Present")],
```

## 1. Business understanding

Households that cannot reliably get enough food have to be found before limited support can be
targeted, so the project was framed as ranking households for follow-up rather than as explaining
food insecurity. Three business objectives (BO1 to BO3) and six hypotheses (H1 to H6) were fixed in
Milestone 1 and are answered in sections 4 and 7 of the final report. The decision that shaped
everything after it: the tool advises an official, it never decides eligibility.

```{r}
phase("Business understanding")
```

## 2. Data understanding

The GHS 2024 arrives as eleven files. Milestone 1 profiled all of them; seven household-level files
were kept, D01 to D03 were dropped as person-level and D11 as a different survey with no shared
household IDs. The phase's most useful finding was a false alarm corrected later: the 256 to 272
"duplicate" household IDs per file were 18-digit IDs read as numbers, not duplicate households.

```{r}
phase("Data understanding")
```

## 3. Data preparation

Each file was cleaned before joining, every treatment logged, and the files joined one at a time
with guarded one-to-one joins that stop rather than silently drop a household. Fifteen placeholder
keys in D05 were repaired by row position and confirmed against province, settlement type and
survey weight. The target is the count of eight food-access items; those items and eight related
columns are excluded from the predictors, which the notebook asserts.

```{r}
phase("Data preparation")
```

## 4. Modelling

Three candidates were tuned with stratified five-fold cross-validation on the training set only:
regularised multinomial logistic regression, a decision tree and a random forest. The three-tier
target could not separate its thin middle tier, which was the condition written down in advance for
falling back to a binary screen, so a fourth model - a lasso logistic regression on any food
insecurity - was fitted with the same recipe and became the deployed one.

```{r}
phase("Modelling")
```

## 5. Evaluation

The models were scored once on the untouched 30% test set and compared on how well they rank
households, not on accuracy, which the 69% food-secure majority would flatter. The referral
threshold of 0.24 was chosen on cross-validation under a policy rule agreed beforehand: find at
least 80% of at-risk households at the fewest referrals.

```{r}
phase("Evaluation")
```

## 6. Deployment

Two things reached a user: a nine-page Power BI dashboard for the programme manager setting referral
capacity, and an R/Shiny tool for an official assessing one household or a batch. Both serve the
same workflow object that was evaluated, by the path `validate -> clean -> preprocess -> score`.
Monitoring thresholds, retraining triggers and rollback are in the handover notes.

```{r}
phase("Deployment")
```

## Milestone 4: making it all agree

The final milestone added no new analysis. It merged the two first-iteration dashboards into one
report on the final dataset, assembled the final document, and made every quoted figure traceable:

* `report/M4/merge_final_report.py` builds the report from the three members' parts and asserts the
  section order and the table numbering.
* `report/M4/check_numbers.py` re-asserts every evaluation figure quoted in the report, the slides
  and the dashboard against `data/evaluation/`.
* `report/M4/build_personB_sections.py`, `build_personC_sections.py` and
  `build_ethics_and_ai_log.py` generate the report sections and the ethics and AI log from the data
  files, so no number is typed in by hand.
* `powerbi/M4_Merged_Dashboard/scripts/build.py` assembles the dashboard project and decodes its own
  embedded tables back out to prove they match `data/powerbi/`.
